text: external sectors. Understanding these issues provides the foundation for analyzing the potential role of governments in improving economic performance through public policy, as well as for assessing the possible consequences of inadequate macroeconomic policies. Prevailing and expected aggregate economic conditions are key considerations in business decision-making. A favorable macroeconomic environment is a prerequisite for the success of entrepreneurial projects and for achieving reasonable returns on financial investments. This course provides students with the fundamental tools needed to understand real-world economic developments and their implications for business activity. It also aims to develop students' ability to critically assess economic conditions and macroeconomic policies.

text: SUBJECT DESCRIPTION This course offers an introduction to Organizational Behavior, a field on human differences, emotions, perceptions, behaviors, and interactions within the context of work organizations. More specifically, the topics include personality, attitude, emotion, and motivation at the individual level, as well as leadership, communication, and conflict at the group/team level. This course addresses issues such as understanding individual differences, motivating employees with various needs, leading groups and teams, resolving conflicts in an organizational context and, eventually, building a high-growth and sustainable organization where people will flourish.

text: LEARNING OBJECTIVES - Become a more confident, dynamic, and persuasive presenter. Participants with successful completion of this course should achieve the following objectives: 1. Raise awareness and sensitivity regarding the impact of human-related issues in the workplace. 2. List basic organizational behavior principles and explain how these principles influence human behavior in the workplace. 3. Analyze individual human behavior by using knowledge of personality, attitudes, emotions, and motivations. 4. Understand group behavior elements, such as leadership, power, politics, communication, conflict, and negotiation. 5. Enhance critical thinking skills through case studies, class discussions, and group projects.

Identify patterns in correlated data: trend, seasonality and cycles. Understand and model time series data with exponential smoothing (ETS) and ARIMA models. text: 2. DIMENSIONALITY REDUCTION 2.1. PRINCIPAL COMPONENT ANALYSIS We want to find a low-dimensional representation of the data that captures as much of the • information as possible. PCA seeks a small number of dimensions that are as interesting as possible. • Theoretically*: • The firs principal component 𝑍1 defines a direction in feature space along which the data vary the most • The second principal component is a linear combination of predictors that has maximal variance out of • all linear combinations that are uncorrelated with 𝑍1 Once we have all the PCs we can plot them to against each other in order to produce low- • dimensional views of the data. * NOTE: find mathematical details about calculating principal components in the recommended books. 10

text: 3. MULTILAYER PERCEPTRON Researchers often use Multilayer Perceptrons to solve complex problems stochastically. • This classifier is highly effective in arranging and categorizing input data into different classes, • allowing probability-based predictions and classifying items into multiple categories. Multilayer Perceptrons have the advantage of learning non-linear models and the ability to train • models in real-time (online learning). Other advantages: • It can be used to solve complex nonlinear problems. • It handles large amounts of input data well. • Makes quick predictions after training. • A single-layer perceptron can only learn linear functions, but Multilayered Perceptrons can • also learn non-linear functions. 13

text: 3. MULTILAYER PERCEPTRON 3.2. BACKPROPAGATION – INTRO BP learning is the most popular learning rule for performing supervised learning tasks. • It uses a gradient-search technique to minimize an error function between the desired and • actual network outputs. Thanks to the BP algorithm, MLP can be extended to many layers. The BP algorithm propagates backward the error between the desired signal and the network • output through the network. After providing an input pattern, the output of the network is then compared with a given target • pattern and the error of each output unit calculated. This error signal is propagated backward, and a closed-loop control system is thus established. • The weights can be adjusted by a gradient-descent based algorithm. • 19

text: 3. MULTILAYER PERCEPTRON 3.2. BACKPROPAGATION Backpropagation vs Gradient Descent? To put it plainly, gradient descent is the process of using gradients to find the minimum value of the cost function, while backpropagation is calculating those gradients by moving in a backward direction in the neural network. Judging from this, it would be safe to say that gradient descent relies on backpropagation. 29

text: 1. INTRODUCTION To a computer, an image is just a grid of numbers. A CNN learns to find patterns in that grid (edges, • textures, shapes) and uses them to recognize what the image shows. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are neural networks built around one operation, convolution: a • small filter slides over the image and detects one pattern at a time. They are inspired by the visual cortex, where each neuron responds only to a small region of what the • eye sees. Older methods needed filters designed by hand. A CNN learns its filters from labelled examples, so it • needs little pre-processing. CNNs are behind photo search, face unlock, medical image screening, factory quality inspection and • driver-assistance cameras. 3

Another common problem is that MLPs react differently to an input (images) and its shifted version — they • are not translation invariant. Thus, spatial information is lost when the image is flattened (matrix to vector) into an MLP. STRIDE By default, when we're doing convolution, we move • our window one pixel at a time (stride=1), but sometimes in convolutional neural networks we want to move more than one pixel. We define stride as the step of the filter. • For example, on pooling layers with kernels of size 2 • we will use a stride of 2. text: 3. BUILDING BLOCKS 3.6. ACTIVATION FUNCTION: ReLU ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit): f(x) = max(0, x). Negative values become 0; • positive values pass through unchanged. Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) It is usually applied after each convolution, often after batch normalization. • Without a non-linear function, a stack of layers behaves like one single linear layer and cannot learn complex shapes. Intuition: each value in a feature map says how strongly a pattern is present. • ReLU keeps the positive evidence and drops the negative responses. ReLU is cheap to compute and lets deep networks train faster than older • functions such as sigmoid or tanh. Not every layer uses it: the output layer uses softmax instead, and modern • networks often use variants such as Leaky ReLU or SiLU. 25 Image OCR:

text: 3. BUILDING BLOCKS 3.7. POOLING LAYER Pooling layers reduce the dimensions • of data by combining the outputs of neuron clusters at one layer into a single neuron in the next layer. Local pooling combines small clusters, • tiling sizes such as 2 × 2 are commonly used. Global pooling acts on all the neurons of the feature map. There are two common types of pooling • in popular use: max and average. Max pooling uses the maximum value of each local cluster of neurons in the feature map, while average pooling takes the average value. 26

text: 4. HYPERPARAMETERS & TRAINING 4.2. OVERFITTING AND DROPOUT Dropout Overfitting: the network memorizes the training images and fails on new ones, e.g. 99% accuracy on training data • but 70% on test data. Dropout randomly switches off a share of neurons (often 50%) at each training step, so the network cannot rely on • any single neuron and learns more general features. text: 4. HYPERPARAMETERS & TRAINING 4.3. BATCH NORMALIZATION Problem: as the weights change during training, the values passed between layers keep changing scale, which • slows learning down. Batch normalization rescales a layer's outputs, for each mini-batch, to mean 0 and standard deviation 1. The • network then learns its own scale and shift for each channel. What you gain: • 1. Faster, more stable training, even for very deep networks such as ResNet 2. Higher learning rates can be used 3. Less sensitivity to how the weights are initialized 4. A mild regularization effect, often used together with dropout 35

text: 3. GENERATIVE MODELS 3.2. QUADRATIC DISCRIMINANT ANALYSIS DISCUSSION Why would one prefer LDA to QDA, or viceversa? The answer lies in the bias-variance trade-off. By instead assuming that the K classes share a common covariance matrix, the LDA model becomes linear in x, which means there are Kp linear coefficients to estimate. text: 6. EVALUATION METRICS DISCUSSION When to use precision and recall? Give some examples. PRECISION: Precision is a valid choice of evaluation metric when we want to be very sure of our prediction. For example: If we are building a system to predict if we should decrease the credit limit on a particular account, we want to be very sure about our prediction or it may result in customer dissatisfaction. RECALL: Recall is a valid choice of evaluation metric when we want to capture as many positives as possible. For example: If we are building a system to predict if a person has cancer or not, we want to capture the disease even if we are not very sure. 37 Spring 2023

text: 1. GRADIENT DESCENT Gradient Descent is a general technique for minimizing an error • function. It can be used to optimize many machine learning models, and it has • particularly nice properties for regression and classification. It works by adjusting parameters in the direction of the negative • gradient. The error function is a “surface” in a high-dimensional space. • Depending on where you start you may end up at a local minimum. • How Gradient Descent Works Calculates the gradient of the error function with respect to the • parameters. Updates the parameters in the opposite direction to the gradient. • The step size is determined by the learning rate. • The process is repeated until a minimum or stopping criterion is • reached. 3

text: 1. DECISION TREES 1.3. PROS AND CONS ▲Trees are very easy to explain to people. In fact, they are even easier to explain than linear regression! ▲ Some people believe that decision trees are closer to human decision-making than do the regression and classification approaches seen in previous chapters. ▲ Trees can be displayed graphically, and are easily interpreted even by a non-expert (especially if they are small). ▲ Trees can easily handle qualitative predictors without the need to create dummy variables. ▼ Unfortunately, trees generally do not have the same level of predictive accuracy as some of the other regression and classification approaches. ▼ Additionally, trees can be very non-robust. text: 1. DECISION TREES 1.4. TREES AND KNN Both are non-parametric. This means that the data distribution cannot be defined in a few • parameters. In other words, Decision trees and KNN’s don’t have an assumption on the distribution of the data. Both can be used for regression and classification problems. • Decision tree supports automatic feature interaction, whereas KNN doesn’t. • Decision trees can be faster. KNN tends to be slower with large datasets because it scans the • whole dataset to predict as it doesn’t generalize the data in advance. 14

text: 1. MAXIMAL MARGIN CLASSIFIER 1.2. MAXIMAL MARGIN CLASSIFIER The maximal margin classifier is the separating hyperplane that is • farthest from the training observations. text: 3. SUPPORT VECTOR MACHINES 3.2. THE KERNEL TRICK – STEP 1: MEASURING SIMILARITY To understand the trick we need one ingredient: the inner product (or dot product) of two observations. Multiply them feature by feature and add up the results: ⟨a, b⟩= a₁·b₁ + a₂·b₂ + … + aₚ·bₚ Intuition: the inner product works as a similarity score. text: 3. SUPPORT VECTOR MACHINES 3.2. THE KERNEL TRICK – STEP 5: HOW IS THE SVM TRAINED? Compute the kernel matrix 1 K(xᵢ, xⱼ) for every pair of training points: an n × n table of similarities. This is all the algorithm sees of the data. Solve the optimisation problem The dual problem (step 2) 2 Find one weight αᵢper training point (dual problem, right). Applications ▲Robust to observations far away from the boundary. text: Exercise 3: Is this economy in equilibrium in the short and the medium/long-run? The equilibrium is given by the intersection of AD & AS curves. text: Exercise 4: What is the effect of an Expansionary Monetary Policy? The neutrality of money • In the short run, a monetary expansion leads to an increase in output, a decrease in the interest rate, and an increase in the price level. • In the medium run, the increase in nominal money is reflected entirely in a proportional increase in the price level. The increase in nominal money has no effect on output or on the interest rate. • The neutrality of money in the medium run does not mean that monetary policy cannot or should not be used to affect output.

text: Answer Key 1. Labor force Labor force = 21 million employed + 2 million unemployed = 23 million people 2. Unemployment rate Unemployment rate = (2 million ÷ 23 million) × 100 = 8.7% 3. Labor force participation rate Working-age population = 21 million + 2 million + 17 million = 40 million people Labor force participation rate = (23 million ÷ 40 million) × 100 = 57.5% 4. Explanation People who are not working and are not actively looking for a job are classified as outside the labor force, not as unemployed. To be considered unemployed, a person must be without work, available to work, and actively seeking employment. 57

Cyclical Unemployment • Is correlated with the ups and downs of the business cycle. • The difference between the actual rate and the natural rate. • Cyclical employment can increase or decrease dramatically over a matter of months for two reasons: 1. text: 3. Five Different Kinds of Unemployment 3. The Natural Rate of Unemployment • The natural rate of unemployment is what would prevail if the economy were not in a recession or expansion. • These medium-run changes can be divided into two kinds: •Frictional •Structural • The underlying rates of frictional and structural unemployment change only slowly through time as major, long-lasting features of the economy change. • The natural rate changes only slowly through time and the actual rate of unemployment varies around the natural rate. 21

Frictional Unemployment • Finding a job that you want at a wage that you will accept, and the employer will pay takes time. • This leads to frictional unemployment. • Scarcity of information is one of the causes of frictional unemployment. • In the United States, most of the natural rate of unemployment is frictional. • The labor market operates relative smoothly. • The same is not necessarily true in Europe. 23

Structural Unemployment It has significant costs: • - Loss of economic output. - The unemployed suffer higher levels of stress, higher rates of suicide, and lower rates of measured happiness. • Structural unemployment has been a more serious problem in Europe than in the US because of labor regulations: - Unemployment benefits, minimum wages, unions, and employment protection laws benefit workers. - All of these regulations are more generous and wide-ranging in Europe. - These regulations can increase unemployment rates. 25

text: 4. Wage Determination 2. Efficiency wage theories link the productivity of the efficiency of workers to the wage they are paid. • Firms may want to pay a wage above the reservation wage in order to decrease workers’ turnover and increase productivity. • Firms that see employee morale and commitment as essential to the quality of workers’ work will pay more than those whose activities are routine. • When unemployment is low, firms that want to avoid an increase in quits will increase wages to induce workers to stay with the firms.

text: European Central Bank MONEY DEFINITION M1: a narrow monetary aggregate that comprises currency in circulation plus overnight deposits held with MFIs and central government (e.g. at the post offi ce or treasury). M2: an intermediate monetary aggregate that comprises M1 plus deposits redeemable at a period of notice of up to and including three months (i.e. short-term savings deposits) and deposits with an agreed maturity of up to and including two years (i.e. short-term time deposits) held with MFIs and central government. M3: a broad monetary aggregate that comprises M2 plus marketable instruments, in particular repurchase agreements, money market fund shares and units, and debt securities with a maturity of up to and including two years issued by MFIs. outline_path: Session 9, 10 › • Since the Great Recession, and during the large-scale asset
text: • Since the Great Recession, and during the large-scale asset purchases (Quantitative Easing), central banks built very large balance sheets. • Reserves in the banking system became abundant, far above the levels banks would hold for transaction/liquidity needs alone. • In this situation the classical money supply = money demand logic is no longer a useful operational tool for controlling interest rates. • Small changes in reserve supply don’t have an effect on the interbank rate (because the supply is already so large that bank demand is relatively inelastic). • Central banks move to a floor or so-called “ample reserves” system: they pay interest on reserves. • The interest on reserves (IOR) becomes a key tool. Copyright © 2017 Pearson Education, Inc. All rights reserved. 4-31

text: Traditional (old) cost accounting • Historically, companies produced a limited variety of products. • These companies used few overhead resources to support these simple operations, so indirect (or overhead) costs were a relatively small percentage of total costs. • Managers used simple costing systems to allocate overhead costs broadly in an easy, inexpensive, and reasonably accurate way. • But as product diversity and indirect costs increased, broad averaging led to inaccurate product costs. That’s because simple peanut-butter costing (that’s what it’s called) broadly averages or spreads the cost of resources uniformly to cost objects (such as products or services) when, in fact, the individual products or services use those resources in nonuniform ways.

Session 2 › Traditional (old) cost accounting
Traditional (old) cost accounting • Historically, companies produced a limited variety of products. • These companies used few overhead resources to support these simple operations, so indirect (or overhead) costs were a relatively small percentage of total costs. • Managers used simple costing systems to allocate overhead costs broadly in an easy, inexpensive, and reasonably accurate way. • But as product diversity and indirect costs increased, broad averaging led to inaccurate product costs. That’s because simple peanut-butter costing (that’s what it’s called) broadly averages or spreads the cost of resources uniformly to cost objects (such as products or services) when, in fact, the individual products or services use those resources in nonuniform ways.

text: Traditional (old) cost accounting • Under costing and over costing. Broad averaging often leads to under costing or over costing of products or services: • Product under costing: a product is reported to have a low cost per unit but consumes a higher level of resources per unit. • Product over costing—a product is reported to have a high cost per unit but consumes a lower level of resources per unit. • Under cost products will be underpriced and may even lead to sales that actually result in losses because the sales may bring in less revenue than the cost of resources they use. • Over cost products will lead to overpricing, causing those products to lose market share to competitors producing similar products.

text: Traditional (old) cost accounting • The following example illustrates how averaging can result in inaccurate and misleading cost data (Undercost: James. Overcost: Emma) • Product-cost cross-subsidization means that if a company undercosts one of its products, it will overcost at least one of its other products. Similarly, if a company overcosts one of its products, it will undercost at least one of its other products. Product-cost cross-subsidization is very common when a cost is uniformly spread—meaning it is broadly averaged—across multiple products without managers recognizing the amount of resources each product consumes. text: Refining the costing system There are three main guidelines for refining a costing system: 1. Direct-cost tracing. Identify as many direct costs as is economically feasible. 2. Indirect-cost pools. Expand the number of indirect-cost pools until each pool is more homogeneous. All costs in a homogeneous cost pool have the same or a similar cause-and-effect (or benefits-received) relationship with a single cost driver that is used as the cost-allocation base. 3. Cost-allocation bases. Whenever possible, managers should use the cost driver (the cause of indirect costs) as the cost-allocation base for each homogeneous indirect-cost pool (the effect).

text: Takeaways
embed_text:
Session 2
Takeaways

text: Takeaways • A cost system is mostly about allocating overhead costs (indirect costs) to products • ABC costing is about estimating the overhead transactions (activities) caused by each product (cost object) • Different cost allocation systems cause different profitability estimations • A cost that can be assigned to a product line (direct cost) should be assigned that way • Many companies continue to use direct labor to allocate overhead • Companies may not allocate all costs to products

text: Management Control Concepts
embed_text:
Session 3
Management Control Concepts

text: Management Control concepts • Financial accounting focuses on reporting financial information to external parties such as investors, government agencies, banks, and suppliers based on Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP). • Management accounting is the process of measuring, analyzing, and reporting financial and nonfinancial information that helps managers make decisions to fulfill the goals of an organization. • Cost accounting provides information for both management accounting and financial accounting professionals. Cost accounting is the process of measuring, analyzing, and reporting financial and nonfinancial information related to the costs of acquiring or using resources in an organization.

Management Control concepts • Financial accounting focuses on reporting financial information to external parties such as investors, government agencies, banks, and suppliers based on Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP). • Management accounting is the process of measuring, analyzing, and reporting financial and nonfinancial information that helps managers make decisions to fulfill the goals of an organization. • Cost accounting provides information for both management accounting and financial accounting professionals. Cost accounting is the process of measuring, analyzing, and reporting financial and nonfinancial information related to the costs of acquiring or using resources in an organization.

text: Management Control concepts Management control = managerial accounting: • “The process of obtaining, creating, and analyzing relevant information to help achieve organizational goals”. • “The process by which managers influence other organizational members to implement organizational strategies” (Anthony and Govindarajan, 2007).

text: Support to design the corporate strategy A company’s strategy specifies how the organization matches its own capabilities with the opportunities in the marketplace. In other words, strategy describes how an organization creates value for its customers while distinguishing itself from its competitors. Management accountants work closely with managers to formulate strategies by providing information about the sources of competitive advantage, such as: (1) the company’s cost, productivity, or efficiency advantage relative to competitors (2) the premium prices a company can charge over its costs from distinctive product or service features

text: Market-based transfer prices A perfectly competitive market exists when there is a homogeneous product with buying prices equal to selling prices and no individual buyers or sellers can affect those prices by their own actions. By using market-based transfer prices in perfectly competitive markets, a company can (1) promote goal congruence, (2) motivate management effort, (3) evaluate the performance of subunits, and (4) preserve their autonomy. When supply outstrips demand, market prices may drop well below their historical averages. text: The Budget as a management tool Responsibility and controllability Budgetary slack: the practice of underestimating budgeted revenues or overestimating budgeted costs to make budgeted targets easier to achieve. Stretching targets: they are challenging but must be achievable to exert extra effort but avoiding excess of anxiety or demotivation. Ethics: At no point should the pressure for performance embedded in stretch targets push employees to engage in illegal or unethical practices.

text: Budgeting cycle 1. Managers at all levels take into account the company’s past performance, market feedback, and anticipated future changes to initiate plans for the next period. 2. At the beginning of the fiscal year, senior managers give subordinate managers a frame of reference, a set of specific financial or nonfinancial expectations against which they will compare actual results. 3. During the course of the year, management accountants help managers investigate any deviations from the plansand if necessary, corrective action.

text: Fundamentals: starting with an example • The problem arose because the chefs were paid by quantity (1,20 $/cake) + favourable cost variance, regardless of quality. • The design of the measurement system has to be comprehensive with due consideration of all of the key factors relating to resource consumption, such as material quantity, quality, and price. • Therefore, the management must utilize comprehensive, holistic measurement and appraisal systems that discourage the promotion of one set of metrics that may have an adverse impact on other key dimensions of business performance. • Variance analysis enables managers to evaluate performance and learn after decisions are implemented.

outline_path: Session 10 › Users, Groups and File Ownership
text: Users, Groups and File Ownership ● The file system stores data and metadata, while the OS checks which processes may access them. ● A user account has a numeric user ID (UID). Processes run with user identities, which the OS uses to check access. ● A group has a group ID (GID) and can include several users. Each user can belong to several groups. ● Each file and directory has one owner UID and one group GID. These are metadata associated with its inode. ● In our container, id reports UID 1001 and GID 1001 for analyst. The numbers match here, but identify different things. ● User and group names make these IDs easier to read. Permissions decide what those identities are allowed to do. 2

outline_path: Session 10 › Nine Bits, Three Permission Classes
text: Nine Bits, Three Permission Classes ● Looking at the .bashrc file, -rw-r--r-- starts with - for a regular file, followed by three triplets: rw-, r--, r--. ● The triplets apply to the owner, group and others, in that order. Others means users who match neither owner nor group. ● For a regular file, r allows reading, w allows changing its contents, and x allows execution. A dash means that permission is absent. ● The OS first checks the process’s user identity. If it matches the file owner, only the owner triplet applies. ● Otherwise, a matching group uses the group triplet. If neither matches, the others triplet applies. The triplets are not added together. ● Here, analyst can read and edit .bashrc, while group members and others can read it, provided they can reach its directory. 4

text: Permissions on Directories ● On a directory, r lets a process list entry names, while x lets it look up those names and traverse the directory. ● Directory w, together with x, normally permits creating, renaming and removing entries. File w controls the contents instead. ● A file can therefore be deleted without write permission on that file, if its parent directory permits removal. ● The initial d means directory. Our home (.) is drwxr-x---, so the `others` class of users cannot reach files inside. ● The + on work signals extra access-control information, e.g., an access-control list (ACL). The nine bits may not describe all access rules. 5

outline_path: Session 10 › Inspect Permissions Before Changing Them
text: Inspect Permissions Before Changing Them ● Use id to inspect your user and groups, and ls -l to inspect a file’s owner, group and permissions. ● Use ls -ld data to inspect the directory itself, rather than list its contents. ● An owner can use chmod to change permission bits. For example, on a practice file: chmod u=rw,g=r,o= notes.txt. ● This gives the owner read and write access, the group read access, and others no access. The result is -rw-r-----. ● In chmod, u means owner, g group and o others. a means all three classes, so others and all are different. ● Example: A loading of a csv file that fails with a permission error can reflect missing file read permission or directory search permission. 6

text: sudo Runs a Command as Another User ● sudo runs an authorized command as another user, usually root (UID 0). The system’s policy decides what is allowed. ● In our course container, analyst is allowed to use sudo without a password. Other systems may require a password or deny the command. ● Compare id, sudo id and then id again. The middle command runs as root, while your ordinary shell remains analyst. ● Use sudo -l to see what your account is permitted to run. It describes privileges, not a file’s permission bits. ● Files created by a command run as root can belong to root, which may prevent later edits as analyst. ● The work folder is shared with your computer. Changes there affect shared files, even when the command runs inside the container. 7

outline_path: Session 10 › FAT: How a File Is Found
text: FAT: How a File Is Found ● Storage is divided into pieces of equal size, called clusters. The data of a file occupy one or more clusters. ● The clusters of a file do not have to be next to each other. FAT can use any free cluster, wherever it is, so a file can grow without needing one long empty region. ● The FAT has one entry for each cluster. The entry says which cluster comes next in the same file, or that this cluster is the last one (-1 in the figure). ● The directory entry of a file records two things: the number of its first cluster and the size of the file. ● To read a file, the OS goes to the first cluster, looks up its entry in the table to find the second, and repeats until it reaches the last. This sequence is the FAT chain. ● In the figure, File A starts at cluster 4. The

text: FAT: Costs and Limitations ● Following a chain means reading many table entries. Reading them from disk would be slow, so the OS keeps a copy of the table in RAM, called a cache. ● The cache only speeds up finding where the data are. The data themselves must still be read from storage. ● The table has one entry per cluster, so a larger disk means a larger table and more RAM for the cache. ● Example: A 1 TB disk with 4 KB clusters has about 250 million clusters. At 4 bytes per entry, the table takes about 1 GB, half the RAM of our container. ● When RAM is short, the OS keeps in RAM only the parts of the table in use and reads the rest from disk when needed. ● The last cluster of a file is rarely full, so some space in it stays unused. ● The clusters of a file can be far apart, which slows

text: Alternatives to FAT ● Other file systems avoid the chain used by FAT. ● Some keep, for each file, a list of all its blocks. Others record multiple extents for each file: "start at this block and continue for this many blocks". ● Example: ext4 is a common Linux file system that stores the starting point of a file's extent list in its inode. ● Journaling protects the file system's own records: a. It writes a note of what it is about to do before changing a record. b. It can finish or undo a half-made change after a crash. ● Note: Journaling is not a backup. Data written just before a crash can still be lost. It writes a note of what it is about to do before changing a record. b. It can finish or undo a half-made change after a crash. ● Note: Journaling is not a backup. Data written just before a crash can still be lost. FAT chain: 5 entries Per-file index: 1 list Extent: 1 record 4 → 5 → 6 → 7 → 8 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 start 4, length 5 The same file, stored in blocks 4 to 8, described in three ways 12

text: File System Management and Optimization ● File-system design balances efficiency, space and reliability. ● How large should each allocation block be? ○ Top panel: reading speed. Each block costs one access to the device, so larger blocks bring more data per access. ○ Bottom panel: the share of allocated space that holds data. A 4KB file fills a 4 KB block, 1/2 of an 8 KB and 1/4 of a 16 KB. ○ Choose the block size for the workload: small blocks for many small files, larger blocks for few large files. ● Other decisions: ○ Tracking free space and allocating data. ○ Quotas to control how much storage each user or group can consume. ○ Backups to recover data after deletion, corruption or device failure. ○ Consistency checks and repairs, which can involve data loss. ○ Caching to reduce

outline_path: Session 11 › When Does the Scheduler Run?
text: When Does the Scheduler Run? ● The OS must choose a process to run when: ○ a new process is created: should the parent or the child run? ○ a process exits, or blocks on I/O or on a lock; ○ an I/O interrupt makes a blocked process ready again; ○ a timer interrupt arrives. ● A non-preemptive scheduler lets a process run until it blocks, exits or gives up the CPU. ● A preemptive scheduler can stop a process at a timer interrupt and run another one. Without preemption, a program stuck in an infinite loop would keep the CPU. ● Linux, macOS and Windows are preemptive. Many early batch systems were not. 3

text: Shortest Job First (SJF) ● SJF runs the shortest job first, then the next shortest, and so on. ● A needs 100s, B and C need 10s: SJF runs B, C, then A. Average turnaround (10 + 20 + 120) / 3 = 50s, against 110 s with FIFO. ● When all jobs arrive together, SJF gives the lowest average turnaround: ○ If four jobs of length a, b, c, d run in that order, they finish at a, a+b, a+b+c, and a+b+c+d. ○ The average is (4a + 3b + 2c + d) / 4: the first job counts four times. ● The idea comes from operations research in the 1950s. text: Response Time and Round Robin ● Interactive users care about response time: how long until their job first runs. ● A, B and C arrive together and need 5s each. SJF runs them one after the other: average response time is (0 + 5 + 10) / 3 = 5s. ● Round Robin (RR) runs each job for a predefined time slice, or quantum, and then moves it to the back of the queue. ● With 1s slices: ○ average response (0 + 1 + 2) / 3 = 1s. ○ Average turnaround grows from 10s with SJF to (13 + 14 + 15) / 3 = 14s. ○ RR stretches the time each job stays in the system by interleaving their execution. outline_path: Session 11 › How Long Should a Time Slice Be?
text: How Long Should a Time Slice Be? ● Each switch costs time: the OS saves and restores registers and runs the scheduler, and the next process starts with cold caches. ● With 4ms slices and 1ms per switch, 1ms in 5 is lost: 20% of the CPU. With 100ms slices, about 1%. ● Long slices hurt response time: with 50 ready processes and 100ms slices, the last one can wait 5s. ● This is amortization: pay a fixed cost less often, as when we batch system calls (Lecture 5). ● Tanenbaum suggests 20–50ms as a compromise. Linux aims for slices of a few milliseconds. 1 ms slices 50% lost to switching 4 ms slices 20% lost to switching work 100 ms slices 1% lost to switching work Assumes 1 ms per switch. 11

outline_path: Session 12 › Linux Took a Different Route
text: Linux Took a Different Route ● In 2003, Linux 2.6 introduced the O(1) scheduler, a close relative of MLFQ, with 140 priority levels and a queue for each level. ● Linux calls what it schedules a task: a process, or one thread of a process. OSTEP, and our animations, call them jobs. ● It always ran the first task in the highest-priority non-empty queue. Finding that task took the same time however many tasks were waiting: hence the name O(1). ● Each task sat in one of two sets of queues, active or expired. A task that used up its time slice moved to expired; when active was empty, the two sets swapped. ● Like MLFQ, O(1) guessed from past behavior which tasks were interactive: tasks that often slept got a priority bonus, those that used a lot of CPU got a penalty. ● The guesses were complex

outline_path: Session 12 › CFS: The Task That Is Behind Runs Next

outline_path: Session 12 › Nice and Priorities in Practice
text: Nice and Priorities in Practice ● nice -n 10 python3 train.py starts a program with nice value 10. ● renice -n 15 -p 4242 changes the nice value of the running process 4242. ● An ordinary user can only raise a nice value, i.e., lower the priority. Lowering a nice value needs administrator rights. ● top and htop show the nice value (NI) and the priority (PR = 20 + NI). ● Priorities matter only when processes compete for a core: alone on a core, a nice 19 process runs at full speed. ● Real-time policies, SCHED_FIFO and SCHED_RR, run before normal processes. chrt sets them but it requires administrator rights. ● On a shared server, start long batch jobs with nice, so that interactive users do not notice them. 9

text: Multiple Cores ● Since about 2005, clock speeds have stopped rising: faster chips would get too hot. Core 0 Core 1 Core 2 Core 3 ● Chips add cores instead. ● A laptop has 8–16 cores and a node of our cluster has Cache Cache Cache Cache 256. A single-threaded program uses one core at a time. ● Each core has small, fast caches with copies of recently used data, so it waits less for RAM. Memory (RAM) ● The hardware keeps the caches coherent: ○ When a core writes a value, the other caches drop their old copy: no core reads a stale value. ○ Two cores can still update the same counter at once: i.e., shared data still needs locks (Lecture 5). ● The scheduler now decides which process runs and on which core. 10

outline_path: Session 12 › One Queue for All Cores
text: One Queue for All Cores ● Single-queue scheduling: every core takes its next process from one shared queue. ● It is simple, and it balances the load: no core is idle while processes wait. ● The queue is shared data, so it needs a lock: cores wait for each other to take the next process. With many cores, this does not scale. ● After each time slice, a process goes back to the queue and the next free core picks it up: processes move from core to core and lose cache affinity. text: One Queue per Core ● Multi-queue scheduling: each core has its own queue and policy, e.g., round robin. ● There is no shared lock and processes stay on their core, so it scales and keeps cache affinity. ● The problem is load imbalance. outline_path: Session 13 › Why We Build HPC Clusters
text: Why We Build HPC Clusters ● Some problems are too big for one computer: their data does not fit in one node's memory, or their work would take months on one node. ● Weather forecasts, climate models, drug design, genomics, financial risk and the training of AI models all run on clusters of many nodes. ● Meta trained its Llama 3 language model (405 billion parameters) with 3.8 x 1025 operations, on 16,000 GPUs in 2,000 servers. One 4-CPU job on our cluster would need about 5 million years. ● A cluster divides the work: with N nodes, a job can finish up to N times sooner, but only if its work splits into parts that rarely need to talk to each other (Session 23). ● Your project does the same at a smaller scale: one workload, 8 many cores, a measured speedup. text: Flynn's Taxonomy ● Michael Flynn classified computers in 1966 by how many instruction streams and how many data streams they process at once. ● Real machines combine the classes: a cluster is MIMD, and every core inside it runs SIMD instructions. ● When NumPy adds two arrays, each instruction adds several numbers at once: up to 8 doubles on the processors of our cluster (AVX-512). One data stream Many data streams One instruction SISD: one instruction on one value at SIMD: one instruction on many values at stream a time. The classic single-core once. Vector units in every core (NumPy computer. uses them), GPUs. Many instruction MISD: rare; no common examples. MIMD: independent cores, each running streams its own instructions on its own data. text: Multiply-Add: Two Operations, One Instruction One multiply-add: a * x + b ● A multiply-add computes a * x + b: one multiplication, then one addition. a = 2 x = 3 ● Processors do both with a single instruction, FMA (fused × multiply-add): 2 × 3 + 4 = 10 in one step. one FMA instruction: 6 ● MAC (multiply-accumulate): add each product to a multiply, then add + b = 4 running total, s = s + a[i] * b[i]. ● A matrix product is made of MACs: each result is a row 10 times a column, multiplied pair by pair and added up. ● So Exercise 1 counted 2 x 2000³ operations for a @ a: Accumulate: a row times a column 2000³ multiply-adds, two operations each. s = 0 4 s = 0 + 1*4 = 4 ● The next slide's test does 8 multiply-adds for every × 1 2 3 5 s = 4 + 2*5 = 14 number (a polynomial). s = 14 + 3*6 = 32 6

text: Curious Corner: A Supercomputer in a Chapel ● Since 2005, the Barcelona Supercomputing Center has kept its MareNostrum supercomputers in Torre Girona, a former chapel on the campus of the Polytechnic University of Catalonia. ● MareNostrum 3 (in the photos, 2015): 3,056 nodes with 48,896 cores, connected by an InfiniBand network, in a glass room built inside the chapel. ● The same design as our cluster, at a larger scale: every node is a shared-memory computer, and the nodes together form a distributed-memory machine. ● MareNostrum 4 (2017): 165,888 cores and 390 TB of RAM in its general-purpose part, for 11.15 petaflops (11 million billion operations per second) at 1.3 MW. ● MareNostrum 5, a European (EuroHPC) supercomputer, has been running since December 2023. 19

text: Computing or Waiting? Computing: the CPU is busy all the time ● Before we choose a worker, we ask what the CPU program does most of the time. ● Computing (CPU-bound): ○ loops, calculations, model fits. Waiting: the CPU is free most of the time ○ The program needs a CPU all the time. waiting for the server CPU ● Waiting (I/O-bound): ○ web requests, databases, slow disks. ○ The program needs almost no CPU, it waits for somebody else (Lecture 11). ● The two types of workload need different workers. We start with waiting. 6

text: Python Threads: threading import threading main thread A def hello(name): print("hello from", name) thread B thread C workers = [threading.Thread(target=hello, thread D args=(name,)) for name in ["A", "B", "C", "D"]] start() join() for t in workers: t.start() for t in workers: t.join() ● Thread(target=f, args=...) creates a thread that will run f. Nothing runs yet. ● start() starts the thread and returns at once, so the main thread goes on. ● join() waits until that thread has finished. ● A thread cannot hand a return value back. It writes its result to shared memory. 7

That is why four downloads process 1 took 1.00 s. process 2 ● Processes have one GIL each, so they run Python code process 3 at the same time, on different cores. process 4 ● Step through it: Threads in Python, step by step. time Each worker has the same work to do. 12

text: Scenario 1: The Slow Notebook ● Where did performance go?! ○ We are reading 8.4M rows from a CSV file into memory ○ Then transactions["risk"] = transactions.apply(score_row, axis=1) passes every raw to the function score_row. This is equivalent to a Python loop that calls a function 8.4M and store the result into a dedicated dataframe column. A modern CPU does roughly 10⁹–10¹⁰ simple operations per second, yet a plain Python ○ loop over a few million rows can take minutes. ○ The hardware could have done this millions of times over, where did the time go? ○ We are been paying a 10-100x tax without knowing it existed. 12

One line becomes thousands of hidden operations. text: Concatenating Commands ● The pipe command ‘|’ is used to concatenate commands ● Concatenation: the output of a command becomes the input of another command ● Unix philosophy: many extremely fast and efficient, capability-specific tools (i.e., the commands) that can be arbitrarily combined to create complex capabilities. ● Problem: given our sales_2025_sample.csv dataset, what is the region with most records? ● Solution based on the commands we have studied: a. (Optional) skip the headers: tail -n +2 sales_2025_sample.csv b. Extracts the region column: cut -d ',' -f 3 c. Groups identical regions together: sort d. Counts records for each region: uniq -c e. Sorts numerically, largest count first: sort -nr f. Returns the count and region with the most records: head -n 1 ● Question: Which

text: From Commands to Scripts ● Our example pipeline implements a pattern: for a given dataset and region, it extracts the top n selling categories. ● We can write a pipeline for each dataset, region, and value of n, or we can save a generalized version of our pipeline in a reusable script. ● Behind the prompt (i.e., where we input the commands) we have been using there is a programmable runtime environment called ‘shell’. Specifically, we have been using the bash shell. ● In this environment, we can define variables, loops, if/else statements, etc. Thus, for each shell we have a programming language with which we can write scripts. ● A complete overview of the bash programming language is not useful for this course ● We look at how to define variables and use them to generalize our example

text: Shell and Python Work Together ● We don’t have to choose between the shell and Python. They call each other. ● From Python: ○ subprocess.run([...]) runs a shell command and hands back its output ● From the shell: ○ python3 my_script.py runs the Python interpreter as a command ● In this way, we can use each for what it’s best at: the shell to move and filter data, Python to compute on it. ● cd work; vi ptos.py: ● We write a Python program that uses our summarize.sh to get the top five selling categories (shell does the data processing) and then sums the total sold items (python does the calculation). 14

text: What Is An Operating System (OS) ● Hardware: chips, boards, RAM, drives, disks, keyboard, a monitor, etc. ● Software: two modes of operation modes: a. Kernel mode: OS has complete access to all the hardware and can execute any instruction the machine is capable of executing. b. User mode: all other software access only a subset of the machine instructions. ● An OS interfaces to the hardware and provides a base for all the other software ● The user interface is the lowest level of user-mode software, and allows the user to start other programs, such as a Web browser, email reader, or music player. ● Applica user mode software relies on the OS. 3 Image OCR: E-mail reader Music player Web browser User mode User interface program Software Kernel mode Operating system Hardware

text: The Operating System as an Extended Machine ● Hardware programming interfaces are are very complicated, difficult, and inconsistent. ● The OS hides the hardware and present programs (and their programmers) with nice, clean, elegant, consistent, abstractions. ● Example: a. SATA hard disk (HD) HW interface spec: 311 pages spec in 2003, 717 in 2011 b. Disk drivers abstract HW interface exposing functions to read/write disk blocks c. OS abstracts away driver interface exposing functions to create/read/write files ● OS implements usable abstractions for application programmers (not end users!) 4 Image OCR: Application programs Beautiful interface Operating system Awful interface Hardware

text: Time Sharing ● A CPU (or any physical processing unit) can run only one process at a time. ● With only a few physical CPU cores available, how can the OS provide the illusion of a nearly endless supply of cores, i.e., one for each active process? ● OS use time sharing: running one process, then stopping it and running another, and so forth. ● Slicing the available processing time across multiple sequential processes and doing it very fast (1000 times/s), gives the illusion of parallel process execution. ● Question: Do we have a performance penalty compared to running the same processes, each on a dedicated physical core? ● Question: Recall the related notion of space sharing? Do we use it in our laptops and computers? 9

text: Concurrency and Parallelism In Multicore Architectures ● Concurrency: the ability to manage multiple processes whose total execution periods overlap in time, e.g., time-sharing executes P1, then P2, then P1, etc. ● Parallelism: running multiple processes at the exact same time on separate hardware cores or processors ● We have heterogeneous processing units (CPU, GPU, TPU, ...) with multiple cores ● OS use time-sharing to achieve concurrency on a single core, and parallelism to do so on multiple cores at the same time. ● This increases the pool of processes that can be active at the same time, but can slow down each executing process due to the performance of each core ● Note: OS using multiple cores != process using multiple cores. ● We will explore in depth the latter in the second part

text: Process States ● A process can be in different states: ○ Running: executing instructions on a processor. ○ Ready: ready to run but the OS has chosen not to run it at this given moment. ○ Blocked: not ready to run until some other event takes place. E.g., when a process initiates an I/O request to a disk, it becomes blocked and thus some other process can use the processor. ● The OS: ○ Moves a process between the ready and running states, i.e., (de)scheduling. ○ Keeps a process blocked (e.g., when it initiates an I/O operation) until some event occurs (e.g., I/O completion) ○ Moves an unblocked process to the ready state again and then to running again, depending on policies. 17 Image OCR: Descheduled (Running) Scheduled Ready IO: initiate IO: done Blocked Figure 4.2: Process: State

E.g., when a process initiates an I/O request to a disk, it becomes blocked and thus some other process can use the processor. ● The OS: ○ Moves a process between the ready and running states, i.e., (de)scheduling. ○ Keeps a process blocked (e.g., when it initiates an I/O operation) until some event occurs (e.g., I/O completion) ○ Moves an unblocked process to the ready state again and then to running again, depending on policies. 17 Image OCR: Descheduled (Running) Scheduled Ready IO: initiate IO: done Blocked Figure 4.2: Process: State

text: No Such a Thing As a Free Lunch ● Threads share memory. That gives them speed and power… And danger. ● Race condition: a. Definition: two threads read the same value, each modifies it, and the result depends on which thread happened to modify the value first. b. Classic example: two workers each add 1 to a shared counter. Worker A and B reads 10, A adds 1, saves 11, B adds 1, saves 11. The counter ends up at 11, not 12. c. Silent killer: The answer is wrong, but no exception is risen. The program silently makes mistakes that are difficult and time consuming to debug, usually also for a LLM. d. Non-deterministic: the same code on the same data can give a different answer on different runs, e. Timing-dependent: notoriously, they disappear when you add a print statement to investigate them,

text: Why User and Kernel Modes? ● Goal: share one machine safely without trusting every application. ● Protecting the system from potential failures or malicious activities by managing how applications interact with system resources like files, memory, I/O, and network. ● User Mode: a. Isolation: Applications run in user mode within their own virtual memory space. This means one application cannot access or modify the memory of another application. b. Crash Protection: If an application crashes, it does not affect the operating system or other applications, maintaining overall system stability. c. text: Why Do We Need a Boundary? ● Imagine every program could write to the disk directly, with no permission check. a. Any program could overwrite any file, including other users’ files and the OS itself. b. A buggy loop could scribble over the memory of your browser, your bank session, everything. c. Nothing could be shared safely: no multi-user machines, no cluster, no cloud. ● Mechanisms to enable separation of user/kernel modes: a. Applications make requests: they name a service, supply arguments, and receive a value or error. b. The OS kernel configures the rules: it defines valid entry points, process memory mappings, identities, and permissions. c. Hardware enforces the boundary: the CPU and memory-management hardware check what the current code is allowed to do: ■ The processor records

Why Do We Need a Boundary? ● Imagine every program could write to the disk directly, with no permission check. a. Any program could overwrite any file, including other users’ files and the OS itself. b. A buggy loop could scribble over the memory of your browser, your bank session, everything. c. Nothing could be shared safely: no multi-user machines, no cluster, no cloud. ● Mechanisms to enable separation of user/kernel modes: a. Applications make requests: they name a service, supply arguments, and receive a value or error. b. The OS kernel configures the rules: it defines valid entry points, process memory mappings, identities, and permissions. c. outline_path: Session 5 › Kernel Events and the System-call Trap
text: Kernel Events and the System-call Trap ● Three types of events can enter the OS kernel: a. System call: an intentional request made by a running process. E.g., a process calling read(fd, …) asks the kernel to obtain data from a file. b. Exception or fault: an event detected by the CPU while executing the current instruction. E.g., a page fault, divide-by-zero operation, or invalid instruction. c. Interrupt: an event from outside the current instruction stream. E.g., a timer tick, completed disk operation, or arriving network packet. ● System call: a. Setup: placing the system-call number and arguments in the CPU registers. b. Execute a special instruction: requests to entry in protected kernel mode (called trap). c. Hardware changes execution state: the CPU changes privilege and executes

text: Syscalls And Python ● Python often provides both low-level and high-level interfaces: ○ For files, os.open(), os.read(), os.write(), and os.close() closely resemble Unix system calls. The built-in open() and file objects provide a safer and more convenient abstraction. ● We use low-level interfaces when precise control matters: ○ Low-level calls are useful in operating-system tools, servers, runtimes, databases, and embedded software. ● We normally use abstractions for application development as higher-level APIs reduce code and prevent common mistakes. text: Syscalls And Python ● File system calls reveal that files are OS-managed resources. ○ Open a file descriptor (fd) from the OS; read/write transfer bytes; close releases fd. ○ Python file objects hide this lifecycle, but underneath they rely on the same OS services. ● Process system calls explain how programs are created and controlled. ○ On Unix, fork creates a child process, exec replaces a process with another program, wait collects a child’s result, and kill sends a signal. ○ Python exposes these through os, although subprocess and multiprocessing are usually more portable and easier to use. ● Memory calls explain how Python obtains memory from the OS. ○ Operating systems provide mechanisms such as brk and mmap to modify a process’s address space. ○ Python’s interpreter and memory

text: Syscalls And Python ● Network abstractions are ultimately built on sockets: ○ socket, connect, send, and related calls establish endpoints and transfer bytes. ○ Libraries for HTTP, APIs, databases, and distributed systems sit on top of sockets and add protocols, encryption, authentication, timeouts, retries, and data serialization. ● Device calls provide a path to hardware-specific operations: ○ ioctl performs operations that do not fit normal byte-oriented read and write behavior. ○ In Python, it is exposed through fcntl.ioctl() on Unix. ○ Used for terminals, cameras, network interfaces, sensors, or custom drivers, but specialized libraries are usually safer and easier. ● We study system calls even when frameworks usually hide them: ○ They explain what high-level operations actually cost

text: How Much a Syscall Cost? ● A system call does not just ‘call a function’. It stops our program, switches privilege level, enters the kernel, does work, then switches all the way back. ● Typical cost of that round trip? on the order of a microsecond, i.e., a millionth of a second! ● Question: how bad can it be? What if a program makes a few million of them? ● Download lecture_5_notebook.ipynb from blackboard in Supporting Material ● Copy it into your work directory on your laptop (wherever you created it) ● Launch JupyterLab from our container: docker compose up jupyter 21

outline_path: Session 6 › Pages: Memory in Fixed-Size Blocks
text: Pages: Memory in Fixed-Size Blocks ● The OS hands out an address space to each process made of pages, typically each page is 4 KB. ● The OS maintains exclusive access to the physical RAM and organizes the physical RAM in a list of frames of the same size as the pages. ● The OS keeps a page table for each process to track which virtual page maps to which physical frame. ● Note: A page does not have to be in RAM! a. It may be unused by the process, e.g., input data that still need processing b. Parked on disk, e.g., when unused by the process or when the OS is context switching processes. ● The CPU consults this mapping on every memory access, billions of times/s. 8

outline_path: Session 6 › Why Is Translation Not Super Slow?
text: Why Is Translation Not Super Slow? ● The CPU keeps a small, very fast cache of recent translations called the TLB (Translation Lookaside Buffer). ● Programs touch the same few memory pages over and over, so the TLB hit rate is typically well above 99%. ● This is the same principle as caching everywhere else: a. Exploit locality: the TLB cache is local and physically near to the core/CPU b. Optimize the common case: processes hits over and over the same page. ● When code jumps around memory randomly, the TLB cannot help. This is one reason scattered accesses are much slower than sequential ones. More in Part II. 12

outline_path: Session 6 › What If The OS Loses The VIRT Gamble?
text: What If The OS Loses The VIRT Gamble? ● If the process starts writing data to every page it was promised, the transition from VIRT to RES forces the OS into a resource crunch. ● Performance Drop (thrashing phase): a. As the process fills up the physical RAM, the OS scrambles to free up space using our storage drive. b. The OS spends its time moving pages back and forth, between RAM and disk. c. Result: Our system enters a state called thrashing. The mouse cursor freezes, UI elements stop responding, and the entire computer slows to a near-total crawl. ● Out-Of-Memory (OOM) Killer strikes: a. If the swap space fills up too, the next time our process tries to write to a new memory address, the CPU triggers a Page Fault but the OS has zero physical frames left to hand out. b. To save itself

text: Page Eviction and Replacement ● Under memory pressure, the OS evict pages from RAM and reuse their frames, while keeping the pages in their process’s virtual address spaces. ● E.g., the OS discards a. text: Swapping ● The OS moves cold, infrequently accessed pages to swap and reuse their physical frames. outline_path: Session 7 › Out of Memory (OOM) Killer in Linux
text: Out of Memory (OOM) Killer in Linux ● Activation: Triggered when fail to free up memory. ● Goal: Sacrifices offending process to rescue system stability. ● The process that triggers the OOM is not necessarily the process that gets killed ● Computes a per-process "badness" score based on how much memory or swap a process uses of its allocation. ● Userspace can bias that score to make a process ineligible. ● The OOM victim is not necessarily the process that triggered the fatal allocation, not the single biggest memory user. ● Our demo scripts (07_oom_demo.py, 07_oom_multi_demo.py, 07_oom_stall_demo.py) show the basic kill, choice three competing processes of different sizes and protection levels, and a OOM failures with system freeze.

outline_path: Session 7 › Linux vs. Windows/macOS: Two Different Bets
text: Linux vs. Windows/macOS: Two Different Bets ● Windows and macOS generally avoid Linux-style aggressive overcommit ● Windows imposes a memory request limit, and an exceeding request fails not allowing the process to start so no innocent bystander gets killed later. ● macOS leans on memory compression and swap first, but does have a OOM analogue called jetsam ● Jetsam picks processes by priority type (background/idle apps first, foreground apps last) rather than a single computed score ● Neither OS exposes an "opt out of being killed" option as Linux.

outline_path: Session 7 › Linux vs. Windows/macOS: Different Tradeoffs
text: Linux vs. Windows/macOS: Different Tradeoffs ● Linux's overcommit-and-kill-later model maximizes memory sharing across many processes, at the cost of unpredictability unless someone actively tunes priorities. ● Windows/macOS's conservative accounting gives predictable, local failures and a better single-user experience, at the cost of leaving some memory capacity unused. ● Context decides the winner: a. Linux's approach fits multi-tenant servers and container platforms b. Windows/macOS model fits interactive desktops where an allocation simply returning an error is better than a random background app dying. ● Neither is "better", each optimizes for what it’s typical workload needs most: memory utilization versus predictability.

outline_path: Session 8 › 5: Request size and Python buffering
text: 5: Request size and Python buffering ● Using os.read(), we vary the request from 1 byte to 1 MiB while reading the same 6 MB file, so the data stay constant. ● One-byte requests need 6,013,655 Python calls and 1,730.384 ms, while 64 KiB requests need 93 calls and 0.245 ms. ● Fewer iterations repeat less Python and kernel work, which explains the large gain without isolating the cost of a syscall. ● Further gains can shrink or reverse because the same file must still be copied, and larger chunks need more temporary memory. ● Using open() for one-byte reads is 14.6 times faster here because its buffer serves many requests without entering the kernel. ● Request size sets how many bytes we receive, while Python's buffer has a separate capacity of 128 KiB in this container. 5

text: 5: Many files or one combined file ● We load the same 100,000 records from 1,000 small CSV files and from one combined file, then check that both return equivalent data. ● One combined file avoids repeating file opening and CSV-reader setup, which can otherwise dominate many small loads. ● In this run, the combined file loads in 0.06 s rather than 0.368 s, making each load about 6.1 times faster. ● Combining the files first costs 0.749 s, so the 0.308 s saved per later load must repay that preparation. ● Three later loads recover the preparation cost, while a single load would not justify combining the files in this run. ● Consolidation therefore helps when we revisit the data often enough, e.g., while adjusting an analysis or rerunning a report. 6

text: 5: Saving results in batches ● We save the same 5,000 rows using three strategies, so differences in time come from how we organise the writing. ● Reopening for every row takes 0.566 s because each row repeats opening, CSV conversion, writing and closing. ● Keeping the file open reduces the time to 0.423 s, while 5,000 calls to to_csv() still repeat slicing and CSV formatting. ● Keeping it open and writing 500 rows per batch needs only ten to_csv() calls and takes about 0.004 s. ● All three outputs contain identical bytes, showing that batching reduces repeated work while preserving the saved result. ● Batches give the largest saving here, while larger batches can need more memory and delay when new results are saved. 7

outline_path: Session 8 › 6A: Categories can save or cost memory
text: 6A: Categories can save or cost memory ● A category stores each distinct label once and gives every row an integer code, so repeated labels can use less memory. ● The region column has only six labels across 100,000 rows, and its storage falls from 1.301 to 0.096 MiB. ● The customer_id column has 60,417 distinct labels, so it must keep a much larger label set as well as 100,000 row codes. ● Its labels and codes use about 1.188 MiB, but a lookup structure adds 2.016 MiB to help Pandas find each label. ● The complete category therefore uses 3.204 MiB rather than 1.335 MiB as text, making it larger despite repeated customer IDs. ● A category helps only when saved label storage outweighs its codes and lookup structures, so measure and verify before converting. 9

outline_path: Session 8 › 6A: Choosing and checking column types
text: 6A: Choosing and checking column types ● We check ranges and missing entries before choosing smaller integer types because those types have limits on the values they can store. ● order_id values from 1 to 100,000 fit int32, while quantity values from 1 to 20 fit int16. ● Repeated labels, including product_id, become categories, while date text becomes date values to reduce storage. ● Prices stay float64 to avoid losing more precision, and customer_id stays text because its category would cost more memory. ● The same nine-column table now uses 4.27 MiB instead of 10.56 MiB, leaving more room for joins, calculations or plots. ● We accept the change after records and regional totals agree with the reference, and we recheck the assumptions for each new file. 10

text: 7: Establishing the regional answer ● Our question is how much revenue each region generated in 2025. All 100,000 sample transactions belong to that year. ● For each transaction, revenue = quantity * unit_price. Summing by region gives the six totals needed for the report. ● The sample fits in memory, so we first use the complete table to establish a reference answer. ● Each alternative must preserve the region labels and agree within half a cent: using less memory is useful only if the answer holds. ● We then change what is retained, i.e., fewer columns, smaller representations, chunks or individual rows. ● This connects loading and preparation to reporting: the required result determines which data must remain in memory. 13

outline_path: Session 8 › 7: Processing chunks and retaining totals
text: 7: Processing chunks and retaining totals ● With CHUNK_ROWS = 10_000, the sample arrives in ten chunks. In this way, we do not load all ten into a list. ● Each chunk contributes regional subtotals. The totals dictionary survives between chunks, so earlier contributions are preserved. ● Once a chunk has contributed, its rows are no longer needed for this sum. Removing their references allows storage to be reused. ● The largest measured chunk uses 0.36 MiB, including revenue. The final six totals agree with the full-table reference. ● With six fixed regions, more rows mean more iterations. Millions of customer groups would make the retained dictionary grow. ● Small chunks repeat work more often, while large chunks need more memory. Note that CHUNK_ROWS counts rows, not the byte requests

text: From RAM to Storage ● Applications need to store and retrieve information. ● RAM alone does not meet every storage requirement: a. A dataset may be larger than the available RAM. b. text: Challenges and a New Abstraction ● Shared storage raises three questions: a. How do we find information? b. How do we control who can access it? c. How do we track which parts of the storage are free? ● The file abstraction gives programs a logical unit for storing information. ● A process executes instructions, an address space holds its memory, and a file can retain its inputs and outputs. ● Processes create files and read or update existing ones through OS interfaces. ● Files on persistent storage can survive a process ending or a system restart. Buffered writes must reach storage to survive power loss. ● The file system organizes files, names and metadata, and works with the OS to manage storage and enforce access rules. 3

text: Text Files Encoding ● ASCII is a minimal encoding, while UTF-8 can represent a much larger set of characters. ● ASCII assigns values 0–127 to letters, digits, punctuation and control characters such as a newline. ● An editor must decode those bytes to display text. text: File Access ● Sequential access reads bytes in order from the current position: ○ A program may stop before the end. To reread a regular file, it can return to an earlier position. ○ This access pattern suits media like magnetic tape. ● Random access lets a program seek to a byte offset before reading or writing: ○ Regular files normally support both sequential and random access. ○ Seeking changes the offset for an open file. It does not itself read data or physically move a disk head. ● Example: an indexed reservation file can locate one record without scanning all earlier records. ● The storage device affects performance and trade offs: ○ An HDD may need to move its head, so scattered access can be slow. ○ An SSD has no moving head, but access size and locality still matter. 11 Image

text: File Operations Common file operations and Linux interfaces Operation Description Create Creates an empty file with metadata. Linux open() with O_CREAT can create it. Delete Removes a name with unlink(). Space can be reclaimed when no hard links or open references remain. Open Checks access and returns a file descriptor for later I/O. It does not read the whole file. Close Releases the file descriptor. Closing alone does not guarantee that writes have reached persistent storage. See p. 25. Read Copies up to the requested bytes into a buffer, normally advancing the offset. Write Writes at the offset, or at the end in append mode. Check how many bytes were written. 13

text: File Operations Common file operations and Linux interfaces Operation Description Append Writes at the end of the file. Linux uses write() on a file opened with O_APPEND, rather than a separate append syscall. Seek Changes the offset used by later reads or writes on a seekable file. It does not itself transfer data. Linux provides lseek(). Get attributes Retrieves metadata such as size, ownership and permissions, e.g., through stat(). Set attributes Changes permitted metadata fields, e.g., chmod() changes permission bits. The process must have authority to make the change. Rename Changes a name or location within the same file system without copying the file’s contents. Across file systems, mv normally copies the data and then removes the source. 14

text: Directory Operations ● Directory operations are available through system calls and library functions. ● These examples apply to Linux in our container. Interface Description Creates a directory. The names . and .. refer to that directory and its parent. mkdir() Removes an empty directory. The special names . and .. do not count as user entries. rmdir() Opens a directory stream through the C library, allowing a program to discover its entries. opendir() Closes the directory stream and releases its resources. closedir() Returns the next entry through the C library, using OS support such as getdents(). readdir() Changes a directory’s name or location within a file system, subject to permissions. rename() 23

text: Directory Operations ● Hard links and symbolic links connect names to files in different ways. Interface Description Creates another name for the same inode within one file system. Both names refer to the link() same data and metadata, so edits through either name affect the same file. A hard link is not a copy. Removes one name and reduces the hard-link count. Other names remain usable. The unlink() data can be reclaimed after the last hard link and the last open reference have gone. ● A symbolic link has its own inode and stores a target path. It can cross filesystem boundaries, but becomes dangling if that path no longer resolves. 24

text: COURSE DESCRIPTION 5 This course offers an introduction to Organizational Behavior, a field on human • differences, emotions, perceptions, behaviors, and interactions within the context of work organizations. More specifically, the topics include personality, attitude, emotion, and motivation at • the individual level, as well as leadership, communication, diversity, and conflict at the group/organizational level. This course addresses issues such as understanding individual differences, motivating • employees with various needs, leading groups and teams, resolving conflicts in an organizational context and, eventually, building a high-growth and sustainable organization where people will flourish. * From the Syllabus

text: LEARNING OBJECTIVES AND SKILLS 6 In this course, students will: • 1. Raise awareness and sensitivity regarding the impact of human-related issues in the workplace. 2. List basic organizational behavior principles and explain how these principles influence human behavior in the workplace. 3. Analyze individual human behavior by using knowledge of personality, attitudes, emotions, and motivations. 4. Understand group behavior elements, such as leadership, power, politics, communication, conflict, and negotiation. 5. Enhance critical thinking skills through case studies, class discussions, and group projects.

text: Describe the Manager’s Functions, Roles, and Skills (1 26 of 4) • Manager: Someone who gets things done through other people in organizations. • Organization: A consciously coordinated social unit composed of two or more people that functions on a relatively continuous basis to achieve a common goal or set of goals. text: Define Job Satisfaction 16 (2 of 5) Job Satisfaction – A positive feeling about a job resulting from an evaluation of its characteristics. • Two approaches for measuring job satisfaction are popular: – The single global rating: “All things considered, how satisfied are you with your job?” Respondents circle a number between 1 and • 5 on a scale from “highly satisfied” to “highly dissatisfied.” – The summation of job facets: . It identifies key elements in a job, such as the nature of the work, supervision, present pay, promotion • opportunities, and relations with coworkers.

text: Define Job Satisfaction 17 (3 of 5) How satisfied are people in their jobs? – Over the last 30 years, employees in the U.S. and most developed countries have generally been satisfied with their jobs. • With the recent economic downturn, more workers are less satisfied. • Satisfaction levels differ depending on the facet involved. • There are cultural differences in job satisfaction.

text: 20 Self-Determination Theory vs. Goal-Setting Theory (1 of 9) • Self-Determination Theory – People prefer to feel they have control over their actions. • Focus on the beneficial effects of intrinsic motivation and harmful effects of extrinsic motivation. • Cognitive evaluation theory - When people are paid for work, it feels less like something they want to do and more like something they have to do. • Proposes that in addition to being driven by a need for autonomy, people seek ways to achieve competence (mastery) and positive connections to others.

outline_path: Session 5 › Self-Determination Theory vs. Goal-Setting Theory (2 of 9)
text: 21 Self-Determination Theory vs. Goal-Setting Theory (2 of 9) Self-Determination Theory • – When extrinsic rewards are used as payoffs for performance, employees feel they are doing a good job. • Eliminating extrinsic rewards can also shift an individual’s perception of why they work on a task from an external to an internal explanation. – Self-determination theory acknowledges that extrinsic rewards can improve even intrinsic motivation under specific circumstances: • Deadlines and specific work standards do, if people believe they are in control of their behavior • Rewards and deadlines diminish motivation if people see them as coercive.

They need to: » make the work interesting, » provide recognition, » link organizational and employee goals, and support employee growth and development.

text: 28 Self-Determination Theory vs. Goal-Setting Theory (9 of 9) • Goal Setting and Ethics • The relationship between goal setting and ethics is quite complex: – If we emphasize the attainment of goals, what is the cost? – Time pressure often increases as we are nearing a goal, which can tempt us to act unethically to achieve it. • We may forgo mastering tasks and adopt avoidance techniques so we don’t look bad, both of which can incline us toward unethical choices.

text: 17 ROLES AND THE PSYCHOLOGICAL CONTRACT (9.3, 1 of 2) Role: a set of expected behavior patterns attributed to someone • occupying a given position in a social unit. Role perception: your own view of how you are supposed to act in a given – situation, learned from the stimuli around you (colleagues, friends, books, films.) Role expectations: how OTHERS believe you should act in that same – situation. The psychological contract: the unwritten agreement between • employee and employer that sets out mutual expectations — what management expects of you, and what you expect of management. It appears in no contract, and it governs most of what people feel about – their job. When it is broken, satisfaction, commitment and performance all fall – immediately.

text: ROLE CONFLICT (9.3, 2 of 2) 18 Role conflict: when an individual faces divergent role expectations, so • that complying with one makes complying with another more difficult. Interrole conflict: when the expectations of your different groups are in – opposition. E.g.: the student who is also an employee and also a son or daughter meets this weekly. Most employees belong simultaneously to an occupation, a work group, a – division and several demographic groups, and those roles do not always agree with each other. The managerial move is not to remove the conflict: It is to make the • expectations explicit. Most role conflict is produced by assumptions nobody has ever said out – loud.
