31 Group Decision Making (5 of 8) • Brainstorming can overcome pressures for conformity. – In a brainstorming session: • The group leader states the problem. • Members then “free-wheel” as many alternatives as they can. • No criticism is allowed. • One idea stimulates others, and group members are encouraged to “think the unusual.”

text: 32 Group Decision Making (6 of 8) • The nominal group technique: – Restricts discussion or interpersonal communication during the decision making process. • Group members are all physically present, but members operate independently. • Permits the group to meet formally but does not restrict independent thinking, as does the interacting group. – Nominal groups outperform brainstorming groups.

text: 33 Group Decision Making (7 of 8) • Steps for a nominal group: 1. Each member independently writes down their ideas on the problem. 2. After this silent period, each member presents one idea to the group. 3. The ideas are discussed for clarity. 4. Each group member rank-orders the ideas. 5. The idea with the highest aggregate ranking determines the final decision.

text: TEAM STATES (10.3) 47 Team states are the shared attitudes and feelings that develop as a • team works together. They shape performance as much as the processes do. MOTIVATION: the team's collective drive to accomplish the task. – TEAM EFFICACY: the shared belief that the team can succeed. Success – produces it, and it then produces more success. TEAM IDENTITY: how far members feel the team is part of who they are. – Strong identity means better performance and more satisfied members. TEAM COHESION: members emotionally drawn to one another and – committed to staying. TEAM TRUST: willingness to be vulnerable to the actions of the other – members. The hardest to build and the quickest to lose.

text: 48 HOW ORGANIZATIONS CREATE TEAM PLAYERS (10.4) SELECTING: hire for the interpersonal skills that teamwork requires, • not only the technical ones. Some organizations use cluster hiring - recruiting a group of people together rather than one at a time. TRAINING: teamwork skills can be developed. Workshops on • problem solving, communication, negotiation, conflict management and coaching produce measurable improvement. REWARDING: if the reward system recognizes only individual • contribution, you will get individual behavior whatever you say about teamwork. The honest summary: organizations ask for teamwork and pay for • individual performance, and then wonder why they do not get teams.

outline_path: Session 10, 11 › WHEN TO USE INDIVIDUALS INSTEAD OF TEAMS (10.5)
text: 49 WHEN TO USE INDIVIDUALS INSTEAD OF TEAMS (10.5) Teams are not free. They cost more time and more coordination than • individual work, and they are not always better. Three questions before you form one: • 1. Can the work be done better by one person? If the task can be completed without input from others, an individual is the right choice. 2. Does the work create a common purpose or set of goals for the group that is more than the sum of individual goals? 3. Are the members genuinely interdependent? Does the success of each depend on the success of the whole? If any answer points away from a team, you are about to pay the full • cost of a team without receiving its benefit.

text: IMPLICATIONS FOR MANAGERS - TEAMS 50 Start with the work to be accomplished, not with the team. Decide • first whether the work needs a team at all. Create the context: adequate resources, effective leadership, a • climate of trust, and a reward system that reflects team contributions. Keep team size small. Large teams are where social loafing lives. • Diversity may hurt performance at first and help it later. Expect the • growing pains instead of concluding that the team does not work. Team leaders should establish a common plan and purpose, and • build team efficacy and a shared mental model. Select, train and reward for teamwork. All three, or none of them • work.

text: 3. Business Strategy 1. CONCEPT OF STRATEGY Some definitions of Business Strategy Common in most definitions: • Strategy gives coherence and direction to the actions. • Involves allocation of resources. • Must give consistency of decisions and actions. Kenneth Andrews - The Concept of Strategy (Irwin, 1971) Strategy is the pattern of objectives, purposes or goals and the major policies and plans for achieving these goals, stated in such a way as to define what business the company is in or is to be in and the kind of company it is or is to be. Alfred Chandler - Strategy and Structure (MIT Press, 1962) The determination of the long-run goals and objectives of an enterprise and the adoption of courses of action and the allocation of resources necessary for carrying out these goals. →

text: S12. Game Theory: Fundamentals 2. Dominant Strategy Equilibrium 1. Dominant strategy equilibrium ▪A strategy is a Dominant strategy for a player if it yields the best payoff (for that player) regardless what strategies the other players choose −Whenever a player has a strategy that is strictly better than any other strategy regardless of the other players’ strategy choices, we say that the first player has a dominant strategy. ▪If all players have a dominant strategy, they will all choose their dominant strategy. text: S12. Game Theory: Fundamentals 4. Nash Equilibrium 3. Nash equilibrium At the Nash equilibrium both players will say: “Given what the other player selected, I am happy with my choice”. Definition: For a two-player game, a Nash equilibrium is an outcome where player 2's strategy is the best response to player 1's strategy and player 1's strategy is a best response to player 2's strategy. ▪A strategy profile is a Nash equilibrium if no player wants to unilaterally deviate to another strategy, given other players’ strategies ▪A Nash Equilibrium is a set of best-response strategies. ▪In a game can be several Nash Equilibriums from 0 to n x n (all the matrix) Nash equilibriums. 25 Ricardo López Pérez, PhD, MBA Strategic Management

text: S12. Game Theory: Fundamentals 6. Exercises at home 2. SIMULTANEOSUS GAMES c) Which firm benefits most from the cooperative outcome? How much would that firm need to offer the other to persuade it to coordinate choices? Compared to the next best opportunity, Firm 1 benefits most from the cooperative outcome [high quality, low quality], as it gains 70=80-10, whereas Firm 2 gains 30=60-30. Therefore Firm 2 will agree to be the one that chooses a high level of quality if Firm 1 “subsidizes” it by transferring 30+ε, where ε can be arbitrarily small. It remains to check whether such a cooperative agreement is legal or not. text: S12. Game Theory: Fundamentals 5 Exercises Exercise 1 Firm 2 Centre North South (3,7) (8,9) (9,8) North Firm 1 (2,10) (7,8) (8,10) South 2. In this game, which strategy (and for which player) can be eliminated as first one? Hence, which are the strategies for player 1 and Player 2 that will remain in the reduced form of the game? What happens if the Prisoners can make another decision also after observing the outcome of the game? outline_path: Session 13 › Tit-for-Tat Strategy (Spanish →“Dónde las dan las toman”)
text: S13. Game Theory: Applied competition 2. Dynamic vs. Static Models Tit-for-Tat Strategy (Spanish →“Dónde las dan las toman”) ▪The mere possibility that you play tit-for-tat is sufficient for competitor to cooperate if the time horizon is long enough. ▪Most managers don’t know how long they will be competing with their rivals, serving to make COOPERATION IS A GOOD STRATEGY, except near the end (called end game problem). Thus in a repeated game, prisoner’s dilemma can have a COOPERATIVE outcome. ▪Industries where only a FEW FIRMS COMPETE under stable demand cost conditions may COOPERATE even though no contractual arrangements are made. E. g. Electric companies. ▪FAILURE TO COOPERATE is the result of rapidly shifting demand or cost conditions, e. g. airlines. 10 Ricardo López Pérez, PhD, MBA

text: S14. Lobster Game 3. Underlying theory of the game Underlying theory of the game ▪Market in which the actions of individual firms materially affect the overall market (and thus other firms’ profits) → oligopoly [Reminder: In perfectly competitive and monopolistically competitive markets, sellers do not believe that their price or output will affect rivals’ prices or output] ▪Lobster game: −3 firms, identical product, forced to charge the same price −only decide on quantity, price = price that “clears the market” given the total produced quantity ▪Cournot NE under Asymmetry of Information ▪Cournot NE with First Mover Advantage ▪Cournot NE with Signalling 13 Ricardo López Pérez, PhD, MBA Strategic Management

text: S14. Lobster Game 3. Underlying theory of the game Observations (2/2) ▪“Out of Equilibrium” scenarios: Firms have an incentive to unilaterally deviate • Firms adjust their quantities and move from the ‘out of equilibrium’ scenario • The adjustment process continues over an iterated game until the Equilibrium quantity is reached ▪The Cournot equilibrium industry output does not maximize industry profits (i.e. it is not pareto optimal; max. for monopoly quantity and price) ▪By maximizing their own profit independently, in Cournot, firms produce more output than if they colluded to maximize profits ▪In the Cournot equilibrium, the market price (and profits) reduces if one of the firms expands its production (unilaterally deviates) 19 Ricardo López Pérez, PhD, MBA Strategic Management

text: S16. Game Theory Applied 1. Mixed Strategies Interpretation • Shooter: Left 20%, Right 80% / Goalie: Left 25%, Right 75% • 𝐸𝑈𝑆hooter (𝐿) = 4(0.25) + 1(0.75) = 1.75 • Given the goalie’s probabilities: • 𝐸𝑈𝑆hooter (𝑅) = 1(0.25) + 2(0.75) = 1.75 Substitute the opponent’s • 𝐸𝑈𝐺oalie (𝐿) = 1(0.20) + 2(0.80) = 1.80 equilibrium • Given the shooter’s probabilities: probabilities into the • 𝐸𝑈𝐺oalie (𝑅) = 5(0.20) + 1(0.80) = 1.80 expected-payoff equations • Each player is indifferent between their two actions: both actions produce the same expected payoff. Therefore, neither player can improve their expected payoff by changing strategy alone • The equilibrium doesn’t predict the outcome of one shot, but rather the probabilities with which players choose their actions across comparable situations.

text: S17. Entry Dynamics 2. The three Bain´s entry conditions Is being Aggressive paying-off? Analyzing game theory suggest: → NO; Remember the Lobster Game • Why? Because the incumbent’s pre-entry pricing does not influence the entrant’s expectations about post-entry competition. But → Why may limit pricing still work? → IT MAY WORK In real life knowledge about industry conditions if often asymmetric. For example: 1. Entrants don´t know IF THE DEMAND IS MEETING THE EXPECTATIONS of customers. Entrant might not be certain whether the incumbent limited the price and whether the market demand is “meeting expectations” or is “below expectations” 2. Entrants don´t know THE COSTS →incumbents knows the costs Entrant might be uncertain whether the incumbent has “typical costs” or “low costs” 24

outline_path: Session 17 › Asymmetry of Information and Signaling Theory
text: S17. Entry Dynamics 5. Asymmetry of Information and Signaling Theory Asymmetry of Information and Signaling Theory Signaling theory is useful for describing behavior when two parties (individuals or organizations) have access to different information. • Typically, one party, the sender, must choose whether and how to communicate (or signal) that information, and the other party, the receiver, must choose how to interpret the signal. • Signaling theory holds a prominent position in a variety of management literatures, including strategic management, entrepreneurship, and human resource management. George Akerlof, Michael Spence, and Joseph Stiglitz received the 2001 Nobel Prize in Economics for their work in information economics. Ricardo López Pérez, PhD, MBA Strategic Management

text: S18. Life Cycle 5. Competitive Advantage in Mature Industries Strategy Implementation in Mature Industries It is challenging to be profitable in mature markets: • Overcapacity and Commoditization increase competitive pressure • Difficult to establish and sustain competitive advantage • Less scope for Differentiation advantage (informed buyers, product standardization, lack of technological change) • Cost advantages are difficult to obtain and sustain (high diffusion of process technology = Firms become homogeneous) • Easier for new entrants to attack established firms (highly developed industry infrastructure together) 40 Ricardo López Pérez, PhD, MBA Strategic Management

text: 3. Performance & Profit Analysis S2. text: 3. Performance & Profit Analysis S2. Value Creation Advantages and Disadvantages of some Performance Indicators ▪Using Revenues to evaluate companies • Pro: Good indicator for evaluating demand. It is proxy for whether customers like (and buy) company’s products and services. • Contra: Does not take into account a company’s costs and expenses. ▪Using Income to evaluate companies • Pro: Takes into account a company’s revenue and expenses and can give hints as to whether a company is profitable. • Contra: Income is only available for the past and does not include future information. ▪Using Market capitalization to evaluate companies • Pro: Takes into account a company’s expected future performance and growth. • Contra: The future is uncertain and shareholders may err in their expectations.

text: 3. Performance & Profit Analysis S2. Value Creation Essential steps for a strategist to evaluate a firm’s profitability 1. Don´t evaluate on just one measure Compare different measures Analyze performance measures along the time. 2. Be careful when comparing measures of firms operating in different sectors Across-sector comparisons may lead to inaccurate conclusions. 3. Take into account that firms can be multi-business organizations They are competing in different sectors and countries. 4. Be aware that financial measures are subject to several measurement errors They must be complemented by additional information about a firm’s strategy. 5 . Appraising of current and past performance Forward–looking measure: Stock market value (volatile!) Backward–looking measure: Accounting ratios

text: Turnover → Represents how many sales a company it is able to generate given the capital invested. This measure tends to vary greatly with industry characteristics because industries that require more capital tend to have a higher denominator. It is a good proxy of value creation, meaning how many sales and volume you are able to generate given your capital. But no cost proxy is inside this measure. Sales = Turnover (or Business numbers) Fix Assets = Long-term tangible piece of property or equipment. Working Capital = Current Assets – Current Liabilities. outline_path: Session 20 › The COSTS of Vertical Integration
text: S20. Vertical Integration 3. Motives for Vertical Integration The COSTS of Vertical Integration 1. Difficult Managing different businesses 2. Differences between different stages of production e.g. : The production of wood is lower that the production of furniture 3. Reduce the development of distinctive capabilities e.g. : Not competing in the markets → Reduce power of getting new capabilities. 4. Incentive problems: lack of “high-powered” incentives. No competition. 5. Limits flexibility → in responding to demand fluctuations → in responding to changes in technology, customer preferences, etc. (But, may be conducive to system-wide flexibility) 6. Increase Compounding risk. All risks concentrated in the same industry. Ricardo López Pérez, PhD, MBA Strategic Management

text: S20. Vertical Integration 3. Motives for Vertical Integration History and vertical integration Before 70s - 80s → Growth phase (companies constantly grew in size) −Firms vertically integrated in order to ensure constant flow of inputs (backward) and sufficient sales (forward) −Technological reasons for integration (e.g. to increase railway safety, firms integrated conductors, station agents, locomotive engineers, etc.) After 70s – 80s → Growth phase is reversed −Trend towards hybrid forms that combine vertical integration with market transactions −Increase of outsourcing and ‘vertical partnerships’ with suppliers (e.g. Toyota’s re-supplying system based on kanban cards) 26 Ricardo López Pérez, PhD, MBA Strategic Management Image OCR: TheVsble Hand The Managerial Revolution inAmerican

outline_path: Session 22 › How do we measure Diversification?
text: S22. Diversification 1. Diversification How do we measure Diversification? • The classical approach to measure product- or market-diversity relies on SIC codes (4 digits industry codes) • Different diversification indices can be created such as Gort Index, Berry index, Herfindahl index (HH). There is a great deal of variation in the way diversification is conceptualized, • Alternative: Patents and trademarks defined, and measured. To Gort (1962) diversification represents the number of markets served. Thereby he used the concept of “heterogeneity of output”. Berry (1974) defined diversification as an increase in the number of industries in which firms are active. 17 Ricardo López Pérez, PhD, MBA Strategic Management Image OCR: SIC Code Example 5713 Major Group Industry Group Industry

text: S22. Diversification 2. Motives for Diversification 1. Growth 1. The desire to escape no growth or declining industries is a powerful motive for diversification (e.g. tobacco, oil, newspapers) 2. Diversification is very successful in generating revenue growth, especially when achieved through acquisitions. 3. Some times is the only way in mature industries. What are consequences in terms of PROFITABILITY? 1. It depends on whether the additional revenue sometimes outweighs the costs for the diversification efforts. 2. Diversification sometimes becomes a cash drain for companies in declining industries. 21 Ricardo López Pérez, PhD, MBA Strategic Management

outline_path: Session 22 › 3. Value creation: Porter’s “three essential tests”
text: S22. Diversification 2. Motives for Diversification 3. Value creation: Porter’s “three essential tests” Industry attractiveness on its own is insufficient to justify diversifying into another industry 1. The attractiveness test → Attractive industry? • The industries chosen for diversification must be structurally attractive or capable of being made attractive 2. The cost-of-entry test → Increase overall profits? • The cost of entry must not capitalize all the future profits 3. The better-off test → Create some competitive advantage or synergies? • Either the new unit must gain competitive advantage from its link with the corporation or vice versa (i.e. some form of “synergy” must be present) 23 Ricardo López Pérez, PhD, MBA Strategic Management

outline_path: Session 22 › How can firms save transaction costs via diversification?
text: S22. Diversification 3. Competitive Advantage & Diversification How can firms save transaction costs via diversification? 1. Internal capital markets • By maintaining a balanced portfolio of cash-generating and cash-using businesses, diversified firms can avoid the costs of using the external capital market • Diversified companies have better access to information on the financial prospects of their different businesses Challenge → Investment allocation within the diversified company is a politicized process (Fosters lobbying and other unproductive activities) 2. Internal labor markets • Transfer employees between their divisions (less hiring and firing, reduce information asymmetries for hiring) • Attract higher caliber of employees by offering a broader set of career opportunities. 27

Internal capital markets • By maintaining a balanced portfolio of cash-generating and cash-using businesses, diversified firms can avoid the costs of using the external capital market • Diversified companies have better access to information on the financial prospects of their different businesses Challenge → Investment allocation within the diversified company is a politicized process (Fosters lobbying and other unproductive activities) 2. Internal labor markets • Transfer employees between their divisions (less hiring and firing, reduce information asymmetries for hiring) • Attract higher caliber of employees by offering a broader set of career opportunities. 27

text: S22. Diversification 4. Performance & Diversification 3. Is there a relation between Diversification and Resources and Capabilities? Diversification and performance depends on the type of RESOURCES & CAPABILITIES owned by a firm (e.g., Helfat & Eisenhardt, 2004; Levinthal & Wu, 2010) • Non scalable Resources & Capabilities →LOW SYNERGIES • Involve opportunity costs • The application of the resource/capability in one product niche limits options to use the resource/capability in another niche (e.g., managerial attention) • Scalable Resources and Capabilities→HIGH SYNERGIES • No opportunity costs (e.g., software, brand) • Simultaneous application in different product niches can even create positive synergies. 33 Ricardo López Pérez, PhD, MBA Strategic Management

Big-bet resource investments (shaping) • Large investment in a tech or business to change current market structure or prevailing norms and assumptions • Such a move persuades and signals commitment to partners, suppliers, customers • Small-scale pivots still possible, but large investments are often irreversible due to the infrastructure that needs to be developed before innovations can even take place • Using or creating uncertainty for one’s own advantage • Famous examples: • Apple iPhone+Ecosystem (iTunes, Appstore) • Tesla EVs+charging network + battery Gigafactories • Microsoft Azure for enterprise software from on-premise licensing to clou-based infrastructure + subscription model 19 Ricardo López

text: S25. Strategy in Turbulent Environments 3.4. Chicken and egg problem 4. Chicken-and-egg problem • Each side waits for the other—solve with price structure (not just price level). • Subsidize the value-creating side (zero or negative price is sometimes optimal). • Potential patterns: free consumers + paid complementors (ad-supported media); free SDKs/dev tools + paid users (enterprise). • Non-price seeding: first-party, exclusive, or hit complements Examples: free players vs. paid servers (Real/Adobe); console bundles; app store fee holidays. text: Business Model Innovation S25.2. Entry Barriers & BMI Why big companies react late? 1. They have great organizational rigidities. They find it hard to adapt their business model or make any changes in its organizational culture. 2. Trust is their defensive barriers and feel no threat until too late. 3. They are confident with their position (current market share) and are confident that the future will be like. 4. The corporate culture is based on respect for the hierarchy, not to the ideas and meritocracy. 26 Ricardo López Pérez, PhD, MBA Strategic Management

What is a Competitive Advantage What is a Competitive Advantage? • Competitive Advantage: Any characteristic of an organization that makes it different from the others, placing it in a superior competitive position. outline_path: Session 29 › The COSTS of Vertical Integration
text: S29. Summary & Conclusions S21.3. Motives for Vertical Integration The COSTS of Vertical Integration 1. Difficult Managing different businesses 2. Differences between different stages of production e.g. : The production of wood is lower that the production of furniture 3. Inhibits development of distinctive capabilities e.g. : Not competing in the markets → Reduce power of getting new capabilities. 4. Incentive problems: lack of “high-powered” incentives 5. Limits flexibility → in responding to demand fluctuations → in responding to changes in technology, customer preferences, etc. (But, may be conducive to system-wide flexibility) 6. Increase Compounding risk. All risks concentrated in the same industry. Ricardo López Pérez, PhD, MBA Strategic Management

Industry Analysis structure–conduct–performance (SCP Model) The structure–conduct–performance (SCP) Model, is a causal theoretical explanation for firm performance through economic conduct. This model has had direct influence on subsequent in models such as Porter´s five forces analysis. The Environment (PEST) has a direct impact on the market structure. The market structure then has a direct influence on the firm's economic conduct, which in turn affects its market performance. Also, Feedback effects occur such that market performance may impact conduct and structure. Also, conduct may affect the market structure. text: S5. Case: US Airline INDUSTRY PERFORMANCE (Recent years) • Increase demand. The economic recovery after the 2008 financial crisis increased demand for air travel, benefiting the industry. • Lower Oil Prices: A sharp decline in oil prices in 2015 and 2016 helped airlines cut operating costs • Improved Cost Efficiency: Airlines improved their cost structures through union, concessions, outsourcing, and investments in fuel-efficient aircraft • Industry Consolidation: Major mergers and acquisitions reduced the number of players. • Capacity Management: Airlines focused on filling existing capacity rather than increasing it. 7 Ricardo López Pérez, PhD, MBA Strategic Management

Case: US Airline Identifying Key Success Factors by Profitability Modeling: Airlines Profitability, as measured by operating income per available seat-mile (ASM), is determined by three factors: yield, which is total operating revenues divided by the number of revenue passenger miles (RPMs); load factor, which is the ratio of RPMs to ASMs; and unit cost, which is total operating expenses divided by ASMs. Thus: Profit Revenue RPMs Expenses =  − ASMs RPMs ASMs ASMs Some of the main determinants of each of these component ratios are the following: • Revenue/RPMs • intensity of competition on routes flown • effective yield management to permit quick price adjustment to changing market conditions • ability to attract business customers • superior

Segmentation, Positioning and Differentiation Segmentation vs. Positioning vs. Differentiation ▪Segmentation = Choice of customers, needs, and geographical areas targeted by a firm (i.e. Where does the firm compete) ▪Positioning = Choice of a favorable position in an industry or market (i.e. cost vs. benefit leadership) ▪Differentiation = Choice how a firm distinguishes its offerings from those of its competitors → Value Proposition ▪Does differentiation imply segmentation? −Not necessarily, depends upon the differentiation strategy Broad −Broad Scope Differentiation–Appealing to what is common Strategy between different customers (Apple, McDonalds, Honda…) Niche −Focused Differentiation–Appealing to what distinguishes Strategy different customer groups

text: S9. Competitive Advantage 1. What is a Competitive Advantage What is a Competitive Advantage? • Competitive Advantage: Any characteristic of an organization that makes it different from the others, placing it in a superior competitive position. It should meet at least 4 criteria: • It must be relevant. • It must be sustainable over time. • It is related to a key success factor. • It should translate into a higher return compared to their opponents or the potential to do so. 4 Ricardo López Pérez, PhD, MBA Strategic Management

text: S9. Competitive Advantage 4. Drivers of Cost Advantage 5. INPUT COSTS The cost of resources used to manufacture the products or services directly impacts the cost. • Location advantages.
